    Choosing the right GW solver

    solver-guide.Rmd

    rfugw ships many Gromov-Wasserstein variants. This guide helps you pick the right one for your problem.

    Setup: two small metric spaces

    We’ll use the same toy data throughout so you can compare outputs directly.

    library(rfugw)

set.seed(1)
ns <- 15
nt <- 18

# Source and target point clouds
X_src <- matrix(rnorm(ns * 2), ns, 2)
X_tgt <- matrix(rnorm(nt * 2), nt, 2)

# Structure matrices (normalized pairwise distances)
C1 <- as.matrix(dist(X_src)); C1 <- C1 / max(C1)
C2 <- as.matrix(dist(X_tgt)); C2 <- C2 / max(C2)

# Feature cost matrix for FGW variants
F_src <- matrix(rnorm(ns * 3), ns, 3)
F_tgt <- matrix(rnorm(nt * 3), nt, 3)
M <- as.matrix(dist(rbind(F_src, F_tgt)))[1:ns, (ns + 1):(ns + nt)]
M <- M / max(M)

    Decision tree 

    Do you have cross-domain features (M)?
├─ No  → GW (structure only)
│   ├─ Need exact solution?       → gromov_wasserstein()
│   └─ Speed matters?             → entropic_gromov_wasserstein()
└─ Yes → FGW (structure + features)
    ├─ Need exact solution?       → fgw_exact_cg()
    └─ Speed matters?             → fgw_entropic()

Are your distributions the same total mass?
├─ Yes, and both marginals fixed  → standard GW / FGW (above)
├─ Yes, but target mass is free   → semirelaxed variants
├─ No, different total mass       → partial or unbalanced variants
└─ No, and you want KL relaxation → fugw_kl()

    Standard GW and FGW

    Both marginals are fixed (source and target weights sum to 1 each). The coupling must satisfy rowSums(plan) == p and colSums(plan) == q.

    # Exact GW (conditional gradient + LP direction)
out_gw <- gromov_wasserstein(C1, C2)
out_gw$gw_dist
#> [1] 0.02171234
    # Entropic FGW (the workhorse)
out_fgw <- fgw_entropic(M, C1, C2, alpha = 0.5, epsilon = 0.05)
out_fgw$fgw_dist
#> [1] 0.1970861
    # Exact FGW (conditional gradient, no regularization)
out_exact <- fgw_exact_cg(M, C1, C2, alpha = 0.5)
out_exact$fgw_dist
#> [1] 0.1647976

    When to use exact vs. entropic: Exact solvers give sparser, more interpretable couplings but scale poorly (LP subproblem at each iteration). Entropic solvers are much faster for problems beyond ~50 points.

    Partial GW and FGW

    Sometimes only a fraction of the mass should be transported—useful when the two domains have different sizes or when you expect only partial overlap.

    The m parameter controls how much mass to transport.

    out_pgw <- partial_gromov_wasserstein(C1, C2, m = 0.5, log = TRUE)
out_pgw$partial_gw_dist
#> [1] 0.0006128621

# Total transported mass
sum(out_pgw$plan)
#> [1] 0.499989
    out_pfgw <- partial_fused_gromov_wasserstein(M, C1, C2, alpha = 0.5, m = 0.7, log = TRUE)
out_pfgw$partial_fgw_dist
#> [1] 0.0769943

    Entropic partial variants are also available:

    out_epgw <- entropic_partial_gromov_wasserstein(C1, C2, m = 0.6, reg = 0.05, log = TRUE)
out_epgw$partial_gw_dist
#> [1] 0.01913513

    Semirelaxed GW and FGW

    In semirelaxed mode, the source marginal is fixed but the target marginal is free—the solver learns it. This is useful when you don’t know the right target distribution a priori (e.g., aligning a subject to a template of unknown density).

    out_sr <- semirelaxed_gromov_wasserstein(C1, C2)
out_sr$srgw_dist
#> [1] 0.007327827

# Source marginal is fixed
summary(rowSums(out_sr$plan))
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#> 0.06667 0.06667 0.06667 0.06667 0.06667 0.06667

# Target marginal was learned
round(out_sr$q, 4)
#>         [,1]
#>  [1,] 0.1333
#>  [2,] 0.0000
#>  [3,] 0.1333
#>  [4,] 0.0667
#>  [5,] 0.0667
#>  [6,] 0.1333
#>  [7,] 0.0667
#>  [8,] 0.0000
#>  [9,] 0.0000
#> [10,] 0.0000
#> [11,] 0.0000
#> [12,] 0.1333
#> [13,] 0.0667
#> [14,] 0.0667
#> [15,] 0.0000
#> [16,] 0.0000
#> [17,] 0.0667
#> [18,] 0.0667

    Entropic semirelaxed variants use mirror descent in KL geometry and are significantly faster:

    out_esr <- entropic_semirelaxed_gromov_wasserstein(
  C1, C2,
  epsilon = 0.05
)
out_esr$srgw_dist
#> [1] 0.01231004
    out_esrf <- entropic_semirelaxed_fused_gromov_wasserstein(
  M, C1, C2,
  alpha = 0.5,
  epsilon = 0.05
)
out_esrf$srfgw_dist
#> [1] 0.1141834

    Fused Unbalanced GW (FUGW)

    When both marginals can deviate from the prescribed distributions, use the unbalanced solver. It relaxes the marginal constraints with KL divergence penalties controlled by reg_marginals.

    out_fugw <- fugw_kl(
  Cx = C1,
  Cy = C2,
  M = M,
  alpha = 0.5,
  epsilon = 0.01,
  reg_marginals = c(10, 10)
)
out_fugw$fugw_cost
#> [1] 0.2281174

    Larger reg_marginals enforces the marginals more strictly (closer to standard FGW). Smaller values allow more deviation.

    # Compare marginals to uniform
cat("Source mass:", sum(out_fugw$pi_samp), "\n")
#> Source mass: 0.9961349
cat("Row marginal range:", range(rowSums(out_fugw$pi_samp)), "\n")
#> Row marginal range: 0.06572043 0.06680493

    Performance tips

    Mixed precision

    For large problems, precision = "mixed" uses single-precision arithmetic for inner Sinkhorn iterations and double for the final objective. This is the default in multialign_fit() and typically 1.5–2x faster with negligible accuracy loss.

    t_double <- system.time(
  fgw_entropic(M, C1, C2, alpha = 0.5, epsilon = 0.05, precision = "double")
)
t_mixed <- system.time(
  fgw_entropic(M, C1, C2, alpha = 0.5, epsilon = 0.05, precision = "mixed")
)
cat("double:", t_double["elapsed"], "s, mixed:", t_mixed["elapsed"], "s\n")
#> double: 0.002 s, mixed: 0 s

    Check frequency

    Increase check_every to reduce the frequency of convergence checks. Each check involves computing a Frobenius norm, so larger values skip more work:

    # Check convergence every 10 outer iterations instead of every 1
out <- fgw_entropic(
  M, C1, C2,
  alpha = 0.5,
  epsilon = 0.05,
  check_every = 10L
)

    Low-rank structure approximation

    For very large structure matrices, the structure_rank parameter enables a low-rank approximation of the GW tensor product, reducing cost from O(n^2 * m) to O(n * m * r):

    out_lr <- fgw_entropic(
  M, C1, C2,
  alpha = 0.5,
  epsilon = 0.05,
  structure_rank = 5L
)
out_lr$fgw_dist
#> [1] 0.197848

    Summary table

    Variant Function Marginals Best for
    Standard GW gromov_wasserstein() Both fixed Small exact problems
    Entropic GW entropic_gromov_wasserstein() Both fixed Fast structure matching
    Standard FGW fgw_exact_cg() Both fixed Exact structure + features
    Entropic FGW fgw_entropic() Both fixed Fast structure + features
    Partial GW/FGW partial_*() Partial mass Incomplete overlap
    Semirelaxed GW/FGW semirelaxed_*() Source fixed, target free Unknown target density
    Unbalanced FUGW fugw_kl() Both relaxed (KL) Noisy, unbalanced data
